## Introduction

We will describe the `HealthWellbeing` dataset so a collaborator can
interpret the five columns and find the original teaching file. By the
end of these 12 minutes, you should be able to read a data dictionary
and explain what the dataset metadata adds.

FAIR stands for **Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable**.
An identifiable source helps people find the data. Access instructions
explain how to obtain it. Structured metadata helps software interpret
it. Definitions, provenance, and reuse terms help people work out
whether the data suit their question. Access can have conditions.
[FAIR Guiding Principles](https://www.go-fair.org/fair-principles/)

Start with the verified file and the `health` object from the data
loading steps. Run the R chunks in the Console from the project root
with *box*, *codebook*, and *dataspice* available. Your instructor can
provide the completed CSV and JSON-LD files for discussion.
[Preparation](00_preparation.qmd#preparation-data)

## Data dictionary

We first load the functions used in this lesson. We label a copy of
the table and keep the downloaded file unchanged.

```{r health-metadata-setup, cache = FALSE}
box::use(
  codebook[codebook_table],
  dataspice[create_spice, write_spice],
  utils[read.csv, write.csv]
)
```

| Column | What it records | Unit or values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `author` | Study label with first author and year | Text |
| `cor` | Pearson correlation of health and well-being | Unitless |
| `n` | Study sample size | Count of observations |
| `population` | Type of study sample | Chronic condition or general population |
| `country` | Country where the study was conducted | Country name |

A row represents one study summary. The supplied snapshot has 29 rows
and no missing values. A zero correlation would describe a study result.
Use a missing value marker such as `NA` for unavailable values in a
future release. The column definitions and original citation come
from the published teaching documentation.
[HealthWellbeing documentation](https://dmetar.protectlab.org/reference/healthwellbeing)

In R, `codebook_table()` combines variable labels with summaries. We
will keep the three columns we need for the exercise and save them as
a CSV.

```{r health-codebook, cache = FALSE}
workshop_dir <- file.path("outputs", "health-wellbeing")
dir.create(workshop_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

labels <- c(
  author = "Study label (first author and year)",
  cor = "Pearson correlation of health and well-being",
  n = "Number of observations in the study",
  population = "Type of study sample",
  country = "Country where the study was conducted"
)

labelled_health <- health
for (column in names(labels)) {
  attr(labelled_health[[column]], "label") <- labels[[column]]
}

dictionary <- codebook_table(labelled_health) |>
  subset(select = c(name, label, n_missing))
write.csv(
  dictionary,
  file.path(workshop_dir, "codebook.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
dictionary
```

## Dataset metadata

A dataset record also needs a title, creator, source, access route, and
any verified licence. *Dataspice* produces a Schema.org Dataset
description in JSON-LD from four CSV files. We will prepare the
worksheets and leave unknown fields blank. The dataset documentation
credits Mathias Harrer for the teaching object. Keep the original
review citation and the book section with the provenance notes.

```{r health-dataspice-templates, cache = FALSE}
metadata_dir <- file.path(workshop_dir, "metadata")
create_spice(dir = workshop_dir)

biblio_path <- file.path(metadata_dir, "biblio.csv")
biblio <- read.csv(biblio_path, fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM")
biblio[1L, ] <- NA
biblio$title <- "HealthWellbeing teaching snapshot"
biblio$description <- paste(
  "Study summaries of health and well-being correlations.",
  "Teaching file from section 4.2.4 of Doing Meta-Analysis with R."
)
biblio$citation <- "Ngamaba, Panagioti, and Armitage (2017)"
biblio$keywords <- "health, well-being, meta-analysis"
write.csv(biblio, biblio_path, row.names = FALSE, na = "")

raw_name <- "healthwellbeing.rda"
data_url <- paste0(
  "https://www.protectlab.org/meta-analysis-in-r/data/", raw_name
)
write.csv(
  data.frame(
    fileName = raw_name,
    name = "HealthWellbeing teaching data",
    contentUrl = data_url,
    encodingFormat = "application/octet-stream"
  ),
  file.path(metadata_dir, "access.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
write.csv(
  data.frame(name = "Mathias Harrer"),
  file.path(metadata_dir, "creators.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)

attributes <- data.frame(
  fileName = raw_name,
  variableName = names(labels),
  description = unname(labels),
  unitText = c(NA, "unitless", "observations", NA, NA)
)
write.csv(
  attributes,
  file.path(metadata_dir, "attributes.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE,
  na = ""
)
```

## Try it yourself

Open `attributes.csv` and add the two population categories to the
description for `population`. Save the edited worksheet, then regenerate
the JSON-LD. Keep `biblio.csv` and `WORKSHOP_NOTES.md` with the JSON-LD so
readers have the original citation, source URL, date of retrieval, and
checksum.

```{r health-dataspice-export, cache = FALSE}
write_spice(path = metadata_dir)
file.exists(file.path(metadata_dir, "dataspice.json"))
```

## Checkpoint {#metadata-checkpoint}

Your codebook has five variables and zero missing values in each.
Look for the dataset title, variable descriptions, and source
download in `metadata/dataspice.json`. Review the draft export for
template placeholders in the coverage fields. Check the provider's
reuse terms before completing the licence field or sharing the data.
With a completed worksheet, explain why someone needs both the
meaning of `n` and the original download link.

Next we will store and retrieve versions of the documented dataset.
[Dataset storage and versioning](05_pins.qmd)
